Functions take inputs (called arguments) and usually provide an output. Below are examples:
```{r}
sqrt(9)
round(3.14159)
round(sqrt(10))
#examples of functions; these all only accept number arguments.
#round() by default rounds to the nearest whole number.
```
Arguments can alter how a function works. For example, the round function can have the digits rounded to change by adding "digits=x". Some functions have preordered arguments see the "seq()" function:
```{r}
round(3.14159)
round(3.14159, digits=2)
print(seq(1, 10, 2))
print(seq(by = 2, from = 1, to = 10))
#seq() by deafault orders 3 arguments in the order of: "from" - the starting number; "to" - the end number; "by" - the increments increasing from the starting number. The order can be changed by typing out the arguments manually.
```
```{r}
print(rep(5, 7))
print(rep(times=7, x=5))
#rep function repeats a variable a set amount of times.
```
Types of variables (x <-): numerical; characters (strings) aka text; logical (TRUE or FALSE). class() function can determine what type of variable something is.
```{r}
x <- 2e-1
print(x)
print(class(x))
y <- "string"
print(y)
print(class(y))
z <- TRUE
print(z)
print(class(z))
```
Creating variables to hold experimental data
```{r}
# my answer
cell_one <- "CX1"
cell_two <- "CX2"
cell_one_treated <- TRUE
cell_two_treated <- FALSE
num_cell_one_before <- 5415
num_cell_one_after <- 1432
num_cell_two_before <- 8123
num_cell_two_after <- 7543

# given answer
cell_id_1 <- "CX1"
cell_id_2 <- "CX2"

treated_1 <- TRUE
treated_2 <- FALSE

n_before_1 <- 5415
n_before_2 <- 8123

n_after_1 <- 1432
n_after_2 <- 7543
```

Part 4: Vectors

```{r}
cell_id_1 <- "CX1"
cell_id_2 <- "CX2"

treated_1 <- TRUE
treated_2 <- FALSE

n_before_1 <- 5415
n_before_2 <- 8123

n_after_1 <- 1432
n_after_2 <- 7543

cell_type <- c(cell_id_1, cell_id_2)
treatments <- c(treated_1, treated_2)
n_before <- c(n_before_1, n_before_2)
n_after <- c(n_after_1, n_after_2)

print(paste(cell_type, treatments, n_before, n_after))
```
each element within a vector has a position, which can be printed using print(vector[n]):
```{r}
nice_food <- c("cheese", "beans", "potatoes")

print(nice_food[1])
```
```{r}
all_my_pets <- c("dog", "horse", "guinea pig", "chicken", "cat")

print(all_my_pets[4])

dinner <- all_my_pets[4]

print(dinner)
```

Data frames are essentially tables of information.
```{r}
my_data_frame <- tibble(
  fruit = c("apple", "pear", "banana"),
  length = c(22, 30, 55),
  weight = c(150, 165, 170)
)


print(my_data_frame)

# notice print() doesn't format the table very nicely, so use gt() instead

gt(my_data_frame)
```

csv files can be read by R.
```{r}
weather <- read_csv("data/weather_data.csv")

gt(weather)
```
